title: Right-Angled Trigonometry

findings.finding: Compare the completed triangles a and c to connect enlargement with unchanged trigonometric ratios.
findings.breakdown: The existing 3–4–5 and 9–12–15 triangles provide a concrete comparison before the constancy investigation.
findings.checked: The corresponding opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse lengths scale by 3. All three ratios agree. The extension uses only the ratios and numerical calculations already available in this topic.
findings.assumptions: Use the corresponding reference angles marked theta.

repair.proposal: After p9-q5-d, add optional parts: (e) What scale factor takes triangle a to triangle c? Answer: 3. (f) Which of the three simplified trigonometric ratios changes between triangles a and c? Answer: none; sine = 3/5, cosine = 4/5 and tangent = 3/4 in both. (g) Triangle a is enlarged by a factor of 4. Write its three trigonometric ratios for the corresponding angle theta. Answer: sine = 12/20 = 3/5, cosine = 16/20 = 4/5, tangent = 12/16 = 3/4.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up explicitly compares corresponding ratios in numerical enlargements.

findings.finding: The final part moves sharply from calculating numerical triangle sides to constructing an equation from two triangles with no known side in either.
findings.breakdown: Parts a and b allow a numerical starting calculation. In part c, students must instead express two horizontal lengths using the unknown shared height, relate their difference to 10, and solve the resulting equation. The preceding numerical calculations do not model that algebraic representation.
findings.checked: Reviewed p25-example-demonstration, p26-teaching-method and p27–p30 practice. The denominator method is taught, and q11-a and q11-b prepare shared-side calculations and subtraction, but no preceding task supplies the transition to representing both lengths algebraically.
findings.assumptions: Students know linear equations and use a degree-mode scientific calculator.

repair.proposal: Add to p30-q11-c: “Express the whole top side and the shorter top side in terms of x using tangent. Their difference is 10. Write and solve an equation.”

findings.doneWhen: Students are prompted to form x/tan 25° − x/tan 50° = 10, while choosing the expressions and solving remain their work.

findings.finding: Extend the existing comparison of reference angles to compare their sine and cosine ratios.
findings.breakdown: The question already uses both acute angles of one triangle, making it a natural place to explain why changing the reference angle exchanges opposite and adjacent.
findings.checked: The acute angles are 54° and 36°. Sine 54° and cosine 36° both round to 0.8090; cosine 54° and sine 36° both round to 0.5878. Side identification and calculator evaluation are already taught. Finding the hypotenuse is unnecessary for this comparison.
findings.assumptions: A degree-mode scientific calculator is available.

repair.proposal: After p29-q9-preference, add optional parts: (d) Calculate sin 54° and cos 36° to four decimal places. Answer: both 0.8090. (e) Calculate cos 54° and sin 36° to four decimal places. Answer: both 0.5878. (f) Explain why the two values in part d are equal using this triangle's sides. Answer: the side opposite 54° is adjacent to 36°, and both ratios divide that side by the same hypotenuse.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up connects the numerical equalities to side roles in the existing triangle.

findings.finding: The first isosceles-triangle trigonometry task requires students to introduce an auxiliary altitude before any preceding instruction shows that construction.
findings.breakdown: The supplied triangle is not right-angled. Students must construct a right triangle and recognise its adjacent side as half the labelled base before applying the taught method. Earlier examples supply their right triangles.
findings.checked: Searched the complete teaching and preceding practice, including p30-q11 and p34-q6. None models splitting an isosceles triangle with an altitude. The altitude in p35-q12-h appears later. Equal-side ticks identify the isosceles triangle but do not supply the construction.
findings.assumptions: Basic isosceles properties are prior knowledge; applying an auxiliary altitude to start a trigonometric solution has not been established.

repair.proposal: Add to p34-q7-b: “Draw a perpendicular from the apex to the base. In this isosceles triangle it bisects the base, so each half is 6 ÷ 2 = 3. Use the right-hand triangle to find theta.”

findings.doneWhen: The construction and origin of the half-base are supplied, leaving ratio selection and inverse trigonometry to students.

findings.finding: Add a short run across the rounding threshold where minutes must carry into degrees.
findings.breakdown: The teaching states the carry rule, but the supplied practice does not expose the boundary between retaining 59 minutes and reaching the next degree.
findings.checked: Reviewed p38-rounding-block, its examples and guided practice, and every part of p39-q4. The proposed answers correctly apply the stated halfway convention and carry rule.
findings.assumptions: Use the booklet's convention of rounding up at 30 seconds.

repair.proposal: After p39-q4-f, retain the existing instruction and add one line: “Predict which answers will reach the next degree before calculating.” Add (g) 42°59′29″, answer 42°59′; (h) 42°59′30″, answer 43°0′; (i) 42°59′31″, answer 43°0′. Follow with unpatterned part (j) 18°23′12″, answer 18°23′. Only seconds vary through g–i; degrees and minutes stay fixed.

findings.doneWhen: The added run exposes both sides of the carry threshold and is followed by an unpatterned item.

findings.finding: The sexagesimal topic combines earlier side and angle methods without an opening review of ratio selection, the two side-equation arrangements and inverse trigonometry.
findings.breakdown: The examples require students to retrieve which ratio applies and whether to multiply, divide or use an inverse function while learning sexagesimal calculator inputs and outputs. These are substantial steps, and the immediately preceding topic rehearses conversion and rounding rather than these trigonometric methods.
findings.checked: The methods are taught in p21, p25–p26 and p31. The p40 and p41 examples use them directly. There is no review in the sexagesimal topic. Conversion and rounding are excluded because p37–p39 prepare them immediately beforehand. The combined-method exception requires rehearsal of the earlier methods.
findings.assumptions: A scientific calculator is available. This is a recall check, not first teaching of the trigonometric methods.

repair.proposal: Before p40-information-block, add four short review items: (a) In a right triangle, relative to theta, the opposite side is 6 and the hypotenuse is 10. Write the relevant trigonometric equation. Answer: sin theta = 6/10. (b) Solve sin 35° = x/12 to 2 d.p. Answer: x = 6.88. (c) Solve cos 42° = 9/x to 2 d.p. Answer: x = 12.11. (d) Solve tan theta = 5/8, giving the acute angle in decimal degrees to 2 d.p. Answer: theta = 32.01°. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The teacher can check ratio selection, numerator and denominator rearrangements, and inverse trigonometry before the sexagesimal examples.

findings.finding: Extend the kite question with a fixed-string run that varies the ground angle.
findings.breakdown: The numerical comparison connects the angle with the vertical height while keeping the hypotenuse fixed.
findings.checked: The proposed heights are 55 sin 30° = 27.5 m, 55 sin 45° ≈ 38.9 m, 55 sin 60° ≈ 47.6 m and 42 sin 37° ≈ 25.3 m. All use methods already taught. No supplied practice run makes this fixed-hypotenuse comparison.
findings.assumptions: As in the existing question, the string's ground endpoint is at ground level and the string is straight.

repair.proposal: After the existing p47-q8 calculation, add one line: “Predict how the height will change before calculating.” Add further parts: (a) A fully extended 55 m string makes an angle of 30° with the ground. Find the height to 1 d.p. Answer: 27.5 m. (b) Repeat for 45°. Answer: 38.9 m. (c) Repeat for 60°. Answer: 47.6 m. Follow with unpatterned part (d): A fully extended 42 m string makes an angle of 37° with the ground. Find the height to 1 d.p. Answer: 25.3 m. Through a–c, only the angle varies.

findings.doneWhen: The optional run compares heights for a fixed string length and ends with an unpatterned calculation.
